clue.text: Very friendly group of people in squat

parts.note: close pals are said to be thick, as in thick as thieves
a set is a social circle or clique

explanation.surface: Close friends crowd together in a squat, an occupied empty building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squat' looks like the noun for an occupied empty building; it is the adjective for a short, stocky build.
explanation.definitionFit: A squat figure is short and broad, which is exactly what a stocky, heavily built person is.

clue.text: Lady's outfit reportedly woolly

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard said, so the words' sound matters

parts.note: a lady's outfit is her suit

explanation.surface: A woman's suit is said to be made of wool.
explanation.definitionFit: Hirsute means hairy or shaggy, as is a woolly coat of fleece or fur.

clue.text: Vulgar John Chapman

definitions.meaning: first meaning: cheap and shoddy, as an adjective
second meaning: a hawker of cheap goods; Jack is a pet form of John and a chapman is an old word for a pedlar

explanation.walkthrough: John Chapman looks like a person's name; it is a playful description of a travelling pedlar, since Jack is the familiar form of John.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheapjack is a seller of shoddy wares, and as an adjective it means tawdry and inferior.

clue.text: Gin and it first combined by a provincial governor

indicators.note: first says which of the pair is placed at the front when they are joined

parts.note: it is slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: A provincial governor mixes himself a gin and Italian vermouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Gin and it looks like the cocktail, gin with Italian vermouth; here the gin is a snare. A satrap governed a province of ancient Persia.
explanation.definitionFit: A satrap was a regional ruler in the ancient Persian empire, appointed to administer a province.

clue.text: After dieting, one may be able to economise

definitions.text: one may be able to economise

parts.note: surface reading: once you have lost weight your waistband needs taking in

parts.words: one may be able to economise
parts.note: setter's reading: the idiom for cutting back on spending

explanation.surface: A slimmer finds their trousers loose after a diet.
explanation.walkthrough: After losing weight you literally pull your belt a notch tighter; the idiom means spending less.
explanation.definitionFit: To tighten one's belt is the idiom for living frugally and cutting back expenses.

clue.text: Politician, a Frenchman with a bit of fire

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for Monsieur, the French title for a man
an ember is a glowing fragment left in a fire

explanation.surface: A French politician is described as having a little fire in his belly.
explanation.definitionFit: A Member of Parliament is a politician, so the short form names an elected representative.

clue.text: Duds make people use bad language

parts.note: men are people
to swear is to curse

explanation.surface: Failures make people curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duds' reads as failures; it is slang for clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Duds is informal for clothes, and menswear is clothing for males sold in shops.

clue.text: Widen carriageway through mountain

indicators.note: something running through another passes inside it, so it sits within

parts.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain, as in Ben Nevis
a carriageway is a road

explanation.surface: Engineers widen a road cut through a mountain pass.
explanation.definitionFit: To broaden something is to make it wider, extending its breadth or scope.

clue.text: In Rome, a matter of importance coming up again

parts.note: res is Latin for a thing or matter
urgent means pressing or important

explanation.surface: An important matter keeps resurfacing in Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Something resurgent is rising once more, reviving after a period of decline.

clue.text: Divine angling club

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a divine is a clergyman, used as a noun
second meaning: the small cudgel an angler uses to kill a landed fish

explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' reads as an adjective describing a heavenly fishing society, but it is a noun for a cleric, and the club is a weapon, not a society.
explanation.definitionFit: A divine is an ordained churchman, and anglers call their fish-killing cosh by the same name as a clergyman.

clue.text: Unstinting surgeon bursting with energy

indicators.note: something bursting is broken apart, so its letters scatter and regroup

parts.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A tireless surgeon is full of vigour and gives his all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unstinting gives freely and lavishly, the same open-handed quality as a liberal giver.

clue.text: Replace one lost by petitioner

indicators.note: something lost by a person is no longer in their possession, so it drops out

parts.note: a suppliant is someone who humbly begs or petitions
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone presenting a petition misplaces a document and needs a replacement.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the I out of SUPPLIANT to leave SUPPLANT.
explanation.definitionFit: To supplant is to take over the position of another, ousting and substituting for them.

clue.text: Speculate about colour these days

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the words following are read from the back

parts.note: red is a colour
now means at the present time

explanation.surface: Someone muses about what colours are fashionable nowadays.
explanation.definitionFit: To wonder is to ponder or ask oneself about something, much as one might guess at an outcome.

clue.text: Some distressed antiques furnish American saloon

indicators.note: some means a part only, so a run of letters is lifted from inside the words

parts.note: the run straddles the two words

explanation.surface: Battered old antiques fill a bar in the American West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saloon' suggests a Wild West bar; here it is the British word for a closed family car, which Americans call a sedan.
explanation.definitionFit: A saloon car in Britain is what US drivers call a sedan, an enclosed four-door motor vehicle.

clue.text: Hesitant chap, Tony's a yesman

indicators.note: a hesitant person wavers back and forth, so these letters are unsettled and reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A timid fellow called Tony always agrees with the boss.
explanation.definitionFit: A sycophant is a flatterer who always agrees with superiors to win favour, like a toady.

clue.text: Canon able to be translated, all things considered

indicators.note: translating turns text into a new form, so these letters are rendered in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A church canon can be rendered into another language, all things considered.
explanation.definitionFit: On balance is the idiom for weighing up every factor before reaching an overall verdict.

clue.text: See ritual being modified without haste

indicators.note: being modified means changed, so these letters are altered in order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A church ceremony is unhurriedly revised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb but is taken as plain letters.
explanation.definitionFit: At leisure means with free time and no hurry, unhurriedly and at one's own pace.

clue.text: He hoards his money before providing support for churchman

parts.note: a miser hoards money
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A tightfisted man saves up before donating to a cleric.
explanation.walkthrough: A miserere, or misericord, is the ledge under a hinged choir-stall seat that a standing cleric leans on.
explanation.definitionFit: The misericord ledge in a choir stall props up a monk or priest during long services.

clue.text: Drug spoken of in Utopia

indicators.note: spoken of means said out loud, so the word's sound counts rather than its spelling

parts.note: cocaine is a drug

explanation.surface: Someone talks of narcotics being freely available in a perfect society.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockaigne is the imaginary land of plenty in medieval legend.
explanation.definitionFit: The Land of Cockaigne was a medieval fantasy realm of luxury and idleness, an ideal place like Utopia.

clue.text: A little money invested in a house may go to one's head

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so it goes within

parts.note: a chalet is a kind of house
P is a penny, a small coin

explanation.surface: Profit from buying a house makes the owner conceited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to one's head' suggests conceit; here it is literal, a wreath worn on the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a garland or wreath worn on the head, so it literally goes there.

clue.text: Share out a fee that's been returned

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a toll is a charge for using a road or bridge

explanation.surface: A refunded payment is divided among several people.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to distribute portions among people, apportioning each their part.

clue.text: Paper folded up — I am getting a cheque

indicators.note: in a down entry up means read from the bottom, so the order is turned

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm
taken as written
a giro is a British state benefit payment, once paid by cheque

explanation.surface: Someone folds up the paper on receiving a cheque.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into decorative shapes.

clue.text: Go ahead — that is certainly good for the digestion

parts.note: surface reading: an emphatic permission to proceed
setter's reading: go is pep, which comes ahead, describing something that aids digestion

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly urges another on, saying it will help the stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: Go means pep, and the word does start with that; the rest of the clue gives no clear letters, so treat it as a playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Peptic describes anything relating to or promoting digestion, from the Greek for cooking or digesting.

clue.text: Fish, one seen in situ

indicators.note: seen in places one thing inside another, so it sits within the second

parts.note: in situ is Latin for in its original place, so situ stands for place
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A fish is observed in its natural habitat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In situ' looks like one phrase, but 'in' is the container signal and 'situ' alone means place.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaice is a flatfish common in European waters, often served battered with chips.

clue.text: Precise training in literary genre given by College Head

indicators.note: in places the first item inside the second, which wraps round it

parts.note: science fiction is a literary genre
PE is physical education, school training

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A college principal offers precise coaching in a particular kind of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: PE is physical education, the school name for gym and games lessons.
explanation.definitionFit: Specific instructions are exact and clearly defined, leaving nothing vague or open to doubt.

clue.text: Everybody in attendance is of normal intelligence

definitions.meaning: first meaning: every single person is present

explanation.surface: A roll call reveals that everyone present is reasonably bright.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying someone is all there means they have their wits intact, and literally it means nobody is missing.

clue.text: A count flabbergasted — he's been presented with a huge bill

definitions.text: he's been presented with a huge bill

indicators.note: someone flabbergasted is thrown into confusion, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An aristocrat is stunned on being handed an enormous invoice.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'huge bill' is not an invoice but a beak.
explanation.definitionFit: This tropical bird has a giant, brightly coloured beak, so nature has handed it an outsize bill.

clue.text: Gossip about race is a lie

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

parts.note: a tale is a fib, as in telling tales
the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: Rumours circulating about a race prove to be false.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattle is idle chatter about other people's affairs, the same as tittle-tattle or rumour.

clue.text: Scoffed under the sheets

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ate heartily, as in tucking in to a meal
second meaning: settled snugly in bed with the bedclothes folded round

explanation.surface: Someone eats a midnight feast in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Scoff here means to eat greedily, a British usage, not to mock.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck in is slang for eating with gusto, and a child is put snugly into bed by folding the covers.
